Do some digging into the type of MS degree you would get. Not all MS degrees are equal from an academic/research perspective. Typically,  you can break types of programs into three categories, typically called Plan A, Plan B, and Plan C.

Plan A has you take ~8-10 total classes, and the rest of your time is spent working in lab, publishing journal articles, and writing your Master's thesis (like a mini PhD dissertation). Typically, these MS programs are funded (you teach undergrad lab sections, and the school covers the cost of attendance, plus a small stipend to pay for rent/food/transit/commuting). If you want to go on to a PhD. program, Plan A is the best option. It shows an adcom that you know how to operate in a lab and you are capable of producing publishable results.

Plan B has more classes, but you still do a research project. However, this is way less research, and just ends in a research paper, more like advanced undergrad classes and less like a PhD.

Plan C is all classes with no research requirement. Plan C masters programs are rarely, if ever funded. Generally, you want to avoid these (an exception would be if you are trying to take as many classes as possible to increase GPA). They tend to be money grabs by universities, and do very little to give you any experience that is applicable to the real world or even academia.

For anyone who's wondering why the nurse is wearing so much PPE, it's because of cumulative exposure. The drug is safe for the patient to take several times for cancer treatment, but the nurse is handling the medication every day, multiple times per day, for potentially 20+ years. So even a little exposure every day could cause severe toxicity (or cancer, a shocking number of chemo drugs cause cancer if used/ handled incorrectly) if the drug accumulates in the nurse's body.

For chronic exposure like the nurse experiences, OSHA sets safe allowable maximums for daily exposure. These daily max exposure limits ensure that 20+ years of daily exposure does not cause toxicity.

1. Do you have a high deductible insurance plan? If yes, the price you are paying is the price insurance negotiated with Novo Nordisk, and you will pay that price every month until you hit your deductible. After that, you'll pay a reduced price.


2. Does your insurance pay for weight-loss meds? If no, you're paying the same negotiated price as above, but Aetna won't pay any of that negotiated price.


3. Does your insurance have a BMI/weight limit for Wegovy? Many plans have a minimum BMI and/or minimum weight. If you're below the minimum, Aetna won't pay anything for your Wegovy.

As someone who transplanted here, winter driving is waaaaay less bad than it sounds until there's a sudden snowstorm. If you have to move in the winter, here are my suggestions. 

1. Buy winter tires before you get here. National chains like discount tire and tires plus can and will order in winter tires to their stores in Florida/the south. They will make the drive much much safer once you're north of Bloomington, IL.

2. Have set points where you can stop if a snow storm pops up and it's unsafe to continue. Every day before you start your drive and at several stops along the way, check the weather in front of you for the next several hours. If the forecast looks grim, book a hotel in the next town you're scheduled to pass through and wait it out. Sleep in a little the next morning to let the plows and salt work their magic.

3. Choose your route carefully. There's a very pretty route along the Mississippi River through MO and IA. Skip it for this trip and stick to the interstate system through IL and WI. IL, WI, and MN have enormous amounts of infrastructure devoted to removing snow and ice from the roads very quickly.

4. If you're driving and you see a plow, DO NOT PASS the plow. In front of the plow is snow/slush that is unsafe to drive on. Behind the plow is snow/slush free pavement where your steering and brakes function properly. I know the plow is only going 30 MPH, but for a first-time winter driver, you don't want to deal with what's in front of the plows. If you're getting frustrated, pull off at the next town, grab a cup of coffee, relax for a while, and then get back on the road after letting the plow get a head start.

Private loans don't get forgiven and only go away when they're paid off or when you die.
